title: Finite-Resolution Limits on Quantum Uniqueness
authors: Seramika Ariwahjoedi, Sameer Ahmad Mir, Mir Faizal
abstract: The Stone-von Neumann theorem makes canonical quantization unique only after one imposes strong continuity of the Weyl translation groups. We show that this continuity assumption cannot be certified by any finite-resolution interrogation of the Weyl relations. A finite protocol probes only finitely many phase-space displacements and bounded expectation values, thereby determining a protocol algebra \(C_S\) generated by a finitely generated subgroup of Weyl translations, but not the regularity of an extension to the full Weyl algebra. Using the polymer representation as a canonical non-regular representation, we prove that for every regular Weyl representation, every normal state, and every finite family of bounded protocol observables, a polymer state reproduces the same expectation values to arbitrary prescribed accuracy. Thus finite agreement with Schrödinger quantum mechanics does not operationally certify the regularity hypothesis entering uniqueness. The result does not assert physical equivalence between regular and polymer quantizations, it identifies where additional input, such as Hamiltonian dynamics, energy regularity, semiclassicality, or a continuum limit, is required to distinguish or select representations. In this precise sense, non-regular polymer kinematics are not excluded by finite Weyl data alone, a point of direct relevance to quantum-gravity motivated quantizations.
summary: This theoretical paper addresses the foundational question of whether finite experimental measurements of Weyl-displacement data can uniquely determine the structure of quantum theory. The authors prove that finite data is insufficient to enforce the strong continuity required for the Stone-von Neumann theorem, demonstrating that non-regular 'polymer' quantizations are indistinguishable from standard quantum mechanics using only finite measurements. This implies that selecting the correct quantum representation requires additional physical input, such as knowledge of the system's dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the strong continuity assumption required by the Stone-von Neumann theorem for canonical quantization uniqueness can be certified using only finite experimental data.
main_result: Finite agreement with Schrödinger quantum mechanics (i.e., finite Weyl data) is insufficient to certify the regularity hypothesis, as non-regular polymer states can reproduce the expectation values of regular states to arbitrary accuracy.
method: The authors use C*algebraic tools, comparing the expectation values derived from a standard regular Weyl representation against those from a canonical non-regular polymer representation using finite protocol algebras.
model_or_system: The system is the canonical quantization of a single degree of freedom, modeled using Weyl operators implementing phase-space translations, comparing the standard regular representation with the non-regular polymer representation.
key_observables: Expectation values of bounded protocol observables (e.g., contractions $A_j$) measured over a finite set of Weyl displacements.
important_parameters: The finite set of displacement labels $S$ and the associated finite protocol algebra $C_S$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is limited to finite-resolution interrogation of the Weyl relations, which only constrains the discrete protocol algebra $C_S$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates that finite control precision restricts access to a discrete set of parameters, allowing regular and non-regular realizations to agree on sampled points within error bars.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the mathematical framework of the Weyl algebra and the Stone-von Neumann theorem, then constructs the polymer representation as a counterexample. It proceeds by showing that the operational compatibility condition derived from finite data is satisfied by both regular and non-regular models.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to foundational quantum physics, particularly quantum gravity, as it sets precise operational boundaries on what can be deduced about the underlying mathematical structure of quantum theory from finite measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Finite-resolution access to Weyl translations (schematic). (a) Finite control precision restricts experimen- tal access to a discrete family of displacement parameters {ξk} ⊂R2 with ξ = (q, p), each realized only within a tol- erance δξ (disks). (b) Finite statistics determine only noisy estimates of an operational quantity, e.g. f(ξ) = ⟨ψ|W(ξ)|ψ⟩, at sampled settings; a regular (strongly continuous) and a non-regular realization can agree on all sampled points within error bars, so strong continuity is not operationally decidable from finite data.
